title: V. By Ilusha’s Bedside
paragraphs: The reader already knows the room where retired captain Snegiryov’s family lived. At that moment it was stuffy and packed with visitors. Several boys were sitting with Ilusha. Like Smurov, all of them were ready to deny that Alyosha had brought them and reconciled them with Ilusha, but that was how it happened. His whole trick had been to bring them to Ilusha one by one, without any “sheepish sentimentality,” making it look casual and unplanned. It was a great comfort to Ilusha in his suffering. It touched him deeply to see the almost tender affection and sympathy of these boys, who had been his enemies. Only Krassotkin was missing, and his absence lay heavy on Ilusha’s heart. Of all his bitter memories, perhaps the bitterest was that he had stabbed Krassotkin, his one friend and protector. Clever little Smurov, who had been the first to make up with Ilusha, thought so too. But Smurov had hinted to Krassotkin that Alyosha wanted to come and see him about something, and Krassotkin cut him short. He told Smurov to tell “Karamazov” at once that he knew best what to do and wanted no one’s advice. If he went to see Ilusha, he said, he would pick his own time, because he had “his own reasons.”

That had been two weeks before this Sunday, and that was why Alyosha had not gone to see him, as he had meant to. He waited, though, and twice more he sent Smurov. Both times Krassotkin gave a curt, impatient no. He sent Alyosha word to stop bothering him, and said that if Alyosha came in person, he, Krassotkin, would not go to Ilusha at all. Smurov did not know until the very last day that Kolya meant to visit Ilusha that morning. Only the evening before, as they were parting, Kolya abruptly told him to wait at home next morning, because they would go to the Snegiryovs’ together. He warned him not to breathe a word about it, since he wanted to drop in casually. Smurov obeyed. Smurov’s notion that Kolya would bring back the lost dog came from something Kolya had let slip, that “they must be asses not to find the dog, if it was alive.” Smurov waited for a good moment and timidly hinted at his guess about the dog, and Krassotkin flew into a violent rage. “I’m not such an ass as to go hunting about the town for other people’s dogs when I’ve got a dog of my own! And how can you imagine a dog could be alive after swallowing a pin? Sheepish sentimentality, that’s what it is!”

For the past two weeks Ilusha had not left his little bed under the icons in the corner. He had not gone to school since the day he met Alyosha and bit his finger. He had fallen ill that same day, though for another month he could sometimes get up and walk around the room and the passage. Lately he had grown so weak that he could not move without his father’s help. His father was terribly anxious about him. He had even stopped drinking and was almost crazy with fear that his boy would die. Often, especially after walking Ilusha round the room on his arm and settling him back in bed, he would run off to a dark corner of the passage. There he would lean his head against the wall and burst into violent weeping, choking back his sobs so that Ilusha would not hear.

Back in the room, he would usually set about amusing and comforting his precious boy. He would tell him stories and funny anecdotes, or imitate comical people he had run into, or even howl and cry like animals. But Ilusha could not stand to watch his father clowning and playing the buffoon. The boy tried not to show how much he hated it, but with an aching heart he saw that his father was an object of contempt. The memory of the “wisp of tow” and that “terrible day” haunted him constantly.

Nina, Ilusha’s gentle, crippled sister, did not like her father’s buffoonery either (Varvara had left some time before to study at the university in Petersburg). The half-witted mother, however, was hugely entertained, and laughed heartily whenever her husband started capering about or acting something out. It was the only thing that could amuse her. The rest of the time she grumbled and complained that everyone had forgotten her now, that nobody showed her any respect, that she was slighted, and so on. In the last few days, though, she had changed completely. She kept looking over at Ilusha’s bed in the corner and seemed lost in thought. She had grown quieter and more silent, and when she cried, she cried softly so that no one would hear. The captain watched the change in her with sad bewilderment. At first the boys’ visits only made her angry, but gradually their cheerful shouting and stories began to divert her. In the end she liked them so much that, had the boys stopped coming, she would have felt miserable without them. When the children told a story or played a game, she laughed and clapped her hands. She called some of them over and kissed them. Smurov was her particular favorite.

As for the captain, the sight of the children in his room, come to cheer up Ilusha, filled his heart with rapturous joy from the start. He even hoped that Ilusha would now throw off his low spirits, and that this would speed his recovery. For all his fear for Ilusha, until lately he had not doubted for one minute that his boy would finally get well.

He greeted his little visitors with reverence and waited on them hand and foot. He was ready to be their horse, and even started letting them ride on his back, but Ilusha did not like the game, so it was dropped. He began buying small treats for them, gingerbread and nuts, and gave them tea and cut sandwiches. It should be said that all this time he had plenty of money. He had taken the two hundred roubles from Katerina Ivanovna, exactly as Alyosha had predicted. Afterwards Katerina Ivanovna heard more about their circumstances and about Ilusha’s illness, and came to see them herself. She got to know the family and managed to win over the half-witted mother. Since then she had given them generous help, and the captain, terrified that his boy might be dying, forgot his pride and accepted it humbly.

All this time Doctor Herzenstube, who had been called in by Katerina Ivanovna, came faithfully every other day. Little came of his visits, and he dosed the invalid mercilessly. But that Sunday morning a new doctor was expected, one who had come from Moscow, where he had a great reputation. Katerina Ivanovna had sent for him from Moscow at great expense. It was not especially for Ilusha but for another purpose, which will be explained in its place later. Since he was here, though, she had asked him to see Ilusha as well, and the captain had been told to expect him. He had not the slightest idea that Kolya Krassotkin was coming, although he had long wished for a visit from the boy Ilusha was pining for.

At the moment when Krassotkin opened the door and came in, the captain and all the boys were standing around Ilusha’s bed, looking at a tiny mastiff pup. It had been born only the day before, though the captain had ordered it a week earlier, to comfort and amuse Ilusha, who was still fretting over the lost and probably dead Zhutchka. Three days before, Ilusha had been told he would be given a puppy, and not just any puppy but a pedigree mastiff (a very important point, of course). Out of delicacy, he tried to pretend he was pleased. But his father and the boys could not help seeing that the puppy only reminded his little heart of the poor dog he had killed. The puppy lay beside him, moving feebly, and he stroked it with his thin, pale, wasted hand, smiling sadly. Plainly he liked the puppy, but ... it wasn’t Zhutchka. If he could have had Zhutchka and the puppy together, he would have been perfectly happy.
“Krassotkin!” one of the boys suddenly cried out. He was the first to see him come in.
Krassotkin’s entrance created a general commotion. The boys stepped back and stood on either side of the bed, so that he could see Ilusha fully. The captain ran eagerly to meet Kolya.
“Please come in ... you’re welcome!” he said hurriedly. “Ilusha, Mr. Krassotkin has come to see you!”

But Krassotkin shook hands with him quickly and at once showed how well he knew the manners of good society. First he turned to the captain’s wife, who sat in her armchair in a very bad temper just then, grumbling that the boys were standing between her and Ilusha’s bed and she could not see the new puppy. With the greatest courtesy he bowed to her, scraping his foot. Then he turned to Nina and, since she was the only other lady present, gave her the same bow. This politeness made an extremely good impression on the deranged lady.
“There, you can tell right away he’s a young man who’s been well brought up,” she said aloud, throwing up her hands. “But our other visitors, they come in one on top of another.”
“What do you mean, mamma, one on top of another? What’s that?” the captain muttered affectionately, though a little worried about her.
“That’s how they ride in. They climb on each other’s shoulders in the passage and prance in like that on a respectable family. Strange sort of visitors!”
“But who’s come in like that, mamma?”
“Why, that boy came in riding on that one’s back, and this one on that one’s.”

Kolya was already standing by Ilusha’s bed. The sick boy went visibly paler. He pushed himself up in bed and stared at Kolya. Kolya had not seen his little friend for two months, and the sight of him overwhelmed him. He had never imagined he would find such a wasted, yellow face, such enormous, feverishly bright eyes and such thin little hands. With grief and surprise he noticed Ilusha’s quick, labored breathing and dry lips. He stepped up close, held out his hand and, nearly overcome, said:

“Well, old man ... how are you?” But his voice failed him. He couldn’t put on an easy manner. His face suddenly twitched and the corners of his mouth shook. Ilusha gave a pitiful little smile, still unable to speak. Something made Kolya lift his hand and stroke Ilusha’s hair.
“Never mind!” he murmured softly, to cheer him up, or perhaps without knowing why he said it. For a minute they were silent again.
“Hey, so you’ve got a new puppy?” Kolya said suddenly, in a perfectly callous voice.
“Ye—es,” Ilusha answered in a long whisper, gasping for breath.

“A black nose, that means he’ll be fierce, a good watchdog,” Kolya remarked gravely and stolidly, as if all he cared about was the puppy and its black nose. In fact he was still straining every nerve not to burst out crying like a child, and whatever he did, he could not get it under control. “When he’s grown, you’ll have to keep him chained up, I’m sure.”
“He’ll be a huge dog!” one of the boys cried.
“Of course he will,” “a mastiff,” “big,” “like this,” “as big as a calf,” several voices shouted.

“As big as a calf, a real calf,” the captain chimed in. “I got one like that on purpose, from the fiercest breed, and his parents are huge and very fierce, they stand this high off the floor.... Sit down here, on Ilusha’s bed, or here on the bench. You’re welcome, we’ve been hoping to see you for a long time.... You were so kind as to come with Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
Krassotkin sat down on the edge of the bed, at Ilusha’s feet. On the way he had perhaps worked out a breezy way to start the conversation, but now he had lost the thread of it entirely.

“No ... I came with Perezvon. I’ve got a dog now, called Perezvon. It’s a Slavonic name. He’s outside ... if I whistle, he’ll run in. I’ve brought a dog too,” he said, suddenly turning to Ilusha. “Do you remember Zhutchka, old man?” he fired the question at him all at once.
Ilusha’s little face quivered. He looked at Kolya in agony. Alyosha, standing at the door, frowned and signaled to Kolya not to mention Zhutchka, but Kolya either did not notice or would not.
“Where ... is Zhutchka?” Ilusha asked, his voice breaking.
“Oh, well, my boy, Zhutchka’s gone. He’s done for!”
Ilusha said nothing, but he fixed his eyes on Kolya again, intently. Alyosha caught Kolya’s eye and made another vigorous sign to him, but Kolya looked away, pretending he hadn’t seen.

“He must have run off and died somewhere. He must have died after a meal like that,” Kolya said without pity, though he seemed a little out of breath. “But I’ve got a dog, Perezvon ... A Slavonic name.... I’ve brought him to show you.”
“I don’t want him!” Ilusha said suddenly.

“No, no, you’ve really got to see him ... it’ll cheer you up. I brought him specially.... He’s the same shaggy kind of dog.... Will you let me call my dog in, madam?” He turned suddenly to Madame Snegiryov, in a strangely excited manner.
“I don’t want him, I don’t want him!” cried Ilusha, with a sad catch in his voice. His eyes had a look of reproach.

“You’d better,” said the captain, getting up from the chest by the wall where he had just sat down, “you’d better ... some other time,” he muttered, but there was no holding Kolya back. He shouted hurriedly to Smurov, “Open the door!” and the moment it was open he blew his whistle. Perezvon came tearing into the room.

“Up, Perezvon, beg! Beg!” shouted Kolya, jumping to his feet, and the dog reared up on its hind legs beside Ilusha’s bed. What came next took everyone by surprise. Ilusha started, lurched hard forward, bent over Perezvon and stared at him, faint with suspense.
“It’s ... Zhutchka!” he cried suddenly, in a voice breaking with joy and pain.
“And who did you think it was?” Krassotkin shouted at the top of his voice, in a ringing, happy tone. He bent down, grabbed the dog and held him up to Ilusha.

“Look, old man, see, he’s blind in one eye and his left ear is torn, exactly the marks you described to me. That’s how I found him, right away. He didn’t belong to anyone!” he explained, turning quickly to the captain, then his wife, then Alyosha, then back to Ilusha. “He lived in the Fedotovs’ back yard. It was his home, but they never fed him. He was a stray that had run away from some village ... I found him.... Now listen, old man, he can’t have swallowed what you gave him. If he had, he’d have died, he’d have had to! So he must have spat it out, since he’s alive. You didn’t see him do it. But the pin pricked his tongue, and that’s why he squealed. He ran off squealing and you thought he’d swallowed it. No wonder he squealed, the skin inside a dog’s mouth is so tender ... tenderer than a man’s, much tenderer!” Kolya cried impetuously, his face glowing and radiant with delight. Ilusha could not speak. White as a sheet, he stared at Kolya with his mouth open and his great eyes almost starting out of his head. Krassotkin had no suspicion of it. If he had known what a disastrous and fatal effect such a moment might have on the sick child’s health, nothing would have made him play such a trick. But Alyosha was perhaps the only person in the room who realized it. As for the captain, he behaved like a small child.
“Zhutchka! It’s Zhutchka!” he cried in a blissful voice. “Ilusha, it’s Zhutchka, your Zhutchka! Mamma, it’s Zhutchka!” He was almost in tears.
“And I never guessed!” cried Smurov, sorry he had missed it. “Bravo, Krassotkin! I told you he’d find the dog, and he has!”
“He has found him!” another boy repeated gleefully.
“Krassotkin’s a star!” cried a third voice.
“He’s a star, he’s a star!” cried the other boys, and they began to clap.

“Wait, wait,” Krassotkin did his best to shout over all of them. “I’ll tell you how it happened, that’s the whole point. I found him, took him home and hid him at once. I kept him locked up there and didn’t show him to anyone until today. Only Smurov has known for the last two weeks, but I told him the dog’s name was Perezvon and he never guessed. Meanwhile I taught the dog all sorts of tricks. You should see everything he can do! I trained him so I could bring you a well-trained dog, in good shape, old man, so I could say to you, ‘See, old man, what a fine dog your Zhutchka is now!’ Haven’t you got a bit of meat? He’ll do a trick for you that’ll make you die laughing. A piece of meat, haven’t you got any?”

The captain ran across the passage to the landlady’s rooms, where their cooking was done. Kolya didn’t want to waste any of the precious time, so in desperate haste he shouted to Perezvon, “Dead!” The dog at once flipped over and lay on his back with all four paws in the air. The boys laughed. Ilusha watched with the same suffering smile, but the one who enjoyed the dog’s performance most was “mamma.” She laughed at him and began snapping her fingers and calling, “Perezvon, Perezvon!”

“Nothing will make him get up, nothing!” Kolya cried triumphantly, proud of his success. “He won’t budge if the whole world shouts at him, but if I call him, he’ll be up in a second. Ici, Perezvon!” The dog leapt up and bounded about, whining with delight. The captain came running back with a piece of cooked beef.

“Is it hot?” Kolya asked quickly, in a businesslike way, taking the meat. “Dogs don’t like hot food. No, it’s fine. Look, everybody, look, Ilusha, look, old man. Why aren’t you looking? I’ve brought him, and he isn’t even looking at him.”

The new trick was to make the dog stand perfectly still with his nose stretched out, and then to lay a tempting bit of meat right on his nose. The poor dog had to stand like that, with the meat on his nose and not moving, for as long as his master pleased, maybe half an hour. But Kolya kept Perezvon like that for only a moment.
“Paid for!” cried Kolya, and in a flash the meat flipped from the dog’s nose into his mouth. The audience, of course, showed delight and amazement.
“Did you really stay away all this time just to train the dog?” exclaimed Alyosha, with a note of reproach he couldn’t hold back.
“Just for that!” answered Kolya, in perfect simplicity. “I wanted to show him off at his best.”
“Perezvon! Perezvon,” Ilusha called suddenly, snapping his thin fingers and beckoning to the dog.

“What is it? Let him jump up on the bed! _Ici_, Perezvon!” Kolya slapped the bed, and Perezvon darted up next to Ilusha. The boy flung both arms around his head, and Perezvon licked his cheek at once. Ilusha snuggled against him, stretched out in the bed and hid his face in the dog’s shaggy coat.
“Dear, dear!” the captain kept saying. Kolya sat down again on the edge of the bed.

“Ilusha, I can show you something else. I’ve brought you a little cannon. You remember I told you about it before, and you said how much you’d like to see it. Well, here it is. I’ve brought it for you.”

And Kolya quickly pulled the little bronze cannon out of his satchel. He was in a hurry because he was so happy himself. At any other time he would have waited for the stir over Perezvon to die down. Now he rushed ahead without any thought for the right moment. “You’re all happy now,” he felt, “so here’s something to make you happier!” He was completely delighted himself.

“I’ve wanted this thing for ages. It’s for you, old man, it’s for you. It belonged to Morozov, he had no use for it, he got it from his brother. I swapped a book from father’s bookcase for it, _A Kinsman of Mahomet or Salutary Folly_, a scandalous book published in Moscow a hundred years ago, before they had any censorship. And Morozov likes that sort of thing. He was grateful to me, too....”

Kolya held up the cannon so everyone could see and admire it. Ilusha sat up and, with his right arm still around the dog, gazed at the toy, enchanted. The excitement grew when Kolya announced that he had gunpowder too, and that they could fire it off at once “if it won’t alarm the ladies.” “Mamma” asked straight away to look at the toy more closely, and she was allowed to. She was delighted with the little bronze cannon on wheels and began rolling it back and forth on her lap. She happily gave permission to fire it, with no idea what she had been asked. Kolya showed the powder and the shot. The captain, being a military man, took charge of loading it and put in a tiny amount of powder. He asked that the shot be kept for another time. They set the cannon on the floor, pointed at an empty part of the room, pushed three grains of powder into the touch-hole and put a match to it. There was a magnificent bang. Mamma was startled but at once laughed with delight. The boys stared in speechless triumph. But the captain, looking at Ilusha, was more enchanted than any of them. Kolya picked up the cannon and presented it to Ilusha at once, along with the powder and the shot.
“I got it for you, for you! I’ve been saving it for you for ages,” he said again, in his delight.

“Oh, give it to me! No, give me the cannon!” mamma began begging like a little child. Her face showed a pitiful fear that she wouldn’t get it. Kolya was thrown off balance. The captain fidgeted uneasily.

“Mamma, mamma,” he ran over to her, “the cannon’s yours, of course, but let Ilusha have it, since it’s a present to him. It’s just as good as yours, though. Ilusha will always let you play with it. It’ll belong to both of you, both of you.”
“No, I don’t want it to belong to both of us. I want it to be all mine, not Ilusha’s,” mamma insisted, on the verge of tears.

“Take it, mother, here, keep it!” Ilusha cried. “Krassotkin, may I give it to my mother?” He turned to Krassotkin with a pleading face, as if afraid Kolya would be hurt by his giving the present to someone else.
“Of course you may,” Krassotkin agreed warmly. He took the cannon from Ilusha and handed it to mamma himself, with a polite bow. She was so touched that she cried.
“Ilusha, darling, he’s the one who loves his mamma!” she said tenderly, and at once started wheeling the cannon back and forth on her lap again.
“Mamma, let me kiss your hand.” The captain darted over to her at once and did so.
“And I’ve never seen such a charming fellow as this nice boy,” said the grateful lady, pointing at Krassotkin.

“And I’ll bring you as much powder as you like, Ilusha. We make our own powder now. Borovikov found out how it’s done—twenty-four parts saltpeter, ten parts sulphur and six parts birchwood charcoal. You pound it all together, mix it to a paste with water and rub it through a fine cloth sieve—that’s the way.”
“Smurov told me about your powder, only father says it’s not real gunpowder,” said Ilusha.
“Not real?” Kolya flushed. “It burns. I don’t know, of course.”
“No, I didn’t mean that,” the captain put in, looking guilty. “I only said real powder isn’t made like that, but it doesn’t matter, it can be made that way.”

“I wouldn’t know, you know best. We lit some in a pomatum jar. It burned splendidly and was gone, with only a tiny bit of ash left. But that was only the paste, and if you rub it through ... but of course you know best, I don’t know.... And Bulkin’s father thrashed him over our powder, did you hear?” he said, turning to Ilusha.
“Yes,” answered Ilusha. He listened to Kolya with huge interest and enjoyment.

“We’d made a whole bottle of it and he kept it under his bed. His father found it. He said it might explode, and thrashed him on the spot. He was going to complain about me to the masters. He’s not allowed to go around with me now. Nobody is allowed to go around with me now. Smurov isn’t either. I’ve got a bad name with everyone. They say I’m a ‘desperate character,’” Kolya smiled scornfully. “It all started with that business on the railway.”

“Ah, we’ve heard about that exploit of yours, too,” cried the captain. “How could you lie still on the track? Is it possible you weren’t the least bit afraid, lying there under the train? Weren’t you frightened?”
The captain flattered Kolya abjectly, with no dignity at all.

“N—not particularly,” Kolya answered offhandedly. “What ruined my reputation here more than anything was that cursed goose,” he said, turning to Ilusha again. He put on an unconcerned air while he talked, but he still couldn’t keep himself in hand, and he kept missing the note he was trying to hold.
“Oh! I heard about the goose!” Ilusha laughed, beaming all over. “They told me, but I didn’t get it. Did they really haul you up before a court?”

“It was the stupidest, most trivial business. They made a mountain out of a molehill, the way they always do,” Kolya began carelessly. “One day I was walking across the market-place, just when they’d driven in the geese. I stopped to look at them. Suddenly a fellow who’s an errand-boy at Plotnikov’s now looked at me and said, ‘What are you staring at the geese for?’ I looked him over. He was a dull, moon-faced fellow of twenty. I’m always on the side of the peasants, you know. I like talking to them.... We’ve fallen behind the peasants—that’s an axiom. I think you’re laughing, Karamazov?”
“No, heaven forbid, I’m listening,” said Alyosha, looking perfectly good-natured, and the touchy Kolya was reassured at once.

“My theory, Karamazov, is clear and simple,” he hurried on again, looking pleased. “I believe in the people, and I’m always glad to give them their due, but I’m not for spoiling them. That’s a _sine qua non_ ... But I was telling you about the goose. So I turned to the fool and said, ‘I’m wondering what that goose is thinking about.’ He gave me a quite blank look. ‘And what is it thinking about?’ he asked. ‘See that cart full of oats?’ I said. ‘The oats are spilling out of the sack, and the goose has put its neck right under the wheel to gobble them up—see?’ ‘I see that fine,’ he said. ‘Well,’ I said, ‘if the cart rolled forward a bit, would it break the goose’s neck or not?’ ‘Sure to break it,’ he said, and grinned from ear to ear, delighted. ‘Come on, then,’ I said, ‘let’s try it.’ ‘Let’s,’ he said. It didn’t take long to set up. He slipped over to the horse’s bridle without being noticed, and I stood off to one side to steer the goose. The owner wasn’t watching, he was busy talking to somebody, so I hardly had to do a thing: the goose stuck its head in after the oats all by itself, under the cart, right under the wheel. I winked at the lad, he gave the bridle a tug, and crack! The goose’s neck was snapped in half. And, just my luck, every peasant there saw us at that very moment and started a row at once. ‘You did that on purpose!’ ‘No, not on purpose.’ ‘Yes, you did, on purpose!’ Then they shouted, ‘Take him to the justice of the peace!’ They dragged me along too. ‘You were in it too,’ they said, ‘you helped, the whole market knows you!’ And for some reason the whole market really does know me,” Kolya added conceitedly. “We all trooped off to the justice’s, and they brought the goose along as well. The fellow was in a great funk and crying, simply blubbering like a woman. And the farmer kept shouting that at this rate you could kill any number of geese. Well, of course, there were witnesses. The justice settled it in a minute: the farmer was to get a rouble for the goose, and the fellow could keep the goose. And he was warned not to try such pranks again. And the fellow went on blubbering like a woman. ‘It wasn’t me,’ he said, ‘he put me up to it,’ and he pointed at me. I replied with perfect calm that I hadn’t put him up to anything, I’d merely stated a general proposition, speaking hypothetically. The justice smiled, and immediately was annoyed with himself for smiling. ‘I’ll report you to your masters,’ he said, ‘so that in future you’ll stop wasting your time on general propositions and sit at your books learning your lessons instead.’ He didn’t report me to the masters, that was a joke, but the story got around and reached their ears. They’ve got long ears, you know! The classics master, Kolbasnikov, was especially scandalized, but Dardanelov got me off again. Kolbasnikov is savage with everybody now, like a green ass. Did you know, Ilusha, he’s just married, and got a dowry of a thousand roubles, and his bride is a regular fright of the first rank and the last degree. The third-class boys wrote an epigram about it:
Astounding news has reached the class, Kolbasnikov has been an ass.
And so on, awfully funny, I’ll bring it to you later. I’ve nothing against Dardanelov. He’s a learned man, no doubt about it. I respect men like that, and not because he stood up for me.”
“But you caught him out about the founders of Troy!” Smurov put in suddenly, plainly proud of Krassotkin at such a moment. The story of the goose had pleased him especially.
“Did you really catch him out?” the captain asked, flatteringly. “On who founded Troy? We heard about that. Ilusha told me at the time.”
“He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!” put in Ilusha. “He only acts like that, but really he’s top in every subject....”
Ilusha looked at Kolya with boundless happiness.

“Oh, all that about Troy is nonsense, a trifle. I consider it an unimportant question,” said Kolya, with haughty humility. By now he had fully regained his dignity, though he was still a little uneasy. He knew he was very worked up, and that he had told the story of the goose, for one thing, with too little restraint, while Alyosha had looked serious and hadn’t said a word the whole time. And little by little the vain boy began to be gnawed by the fear that Alyosha was silent because he despised him, and thought he was showing off. If he dared to think anything like that, Kolya would—
“I regard the question as quite trivial,” he snapped again, proudly.

“And I know who founded Troy,” said a boy who hadn’t spoken before, suddenly, to everyone’s surprise. He had sat silent and seemed shy. He was a pretty boy of about eleven, named Kartashov, and he was sitting near the door. Kolya looked at him with dignified amazement.

The fact was that who had founded Troy had become a secret for the whole school, a secret you could only find out by reading Smaragdov, and nobody had Smaragdov but Kolya. One day, when Kolya had his back turned, Kartashov had quickly opened the Smaragdov that lay among Kolya’s books, and at once hit on the passage about the founding of Troy. That was quite a while ago, but he felt uneasy about it and couldn’t bring himself to announce in public that he too knew who had founded Troy. He was afraid of what might happen, and of Krassotkin somehow shaming him over it. But now he couldn’t help saying it. For weeks he had been longing to.

“Well, who did found it?” asked Kolya, turning to him with haughty superiority. He saw from the boy’s face that he really did know, and he made up his mind at once how to take it. There was, so to speak, a jarring note in the general harmony.

“Troy was founded by Teucer, Dardanus, Ilius and Tros,” the boy rapped out at once, and in the same instant he blushed, blushed so deeply that it hurt to look at him. But the boys stared at him, stared at him for a whole minute, and then all the staring eyes swung round together and fixed on Kolya, who was still looking the bold boy over with scornful calm.
“In what sense did they found it?” he condescended to say at last. “And what does it mean, to found a city or a state? What do they do? Did each of them go and lay a brick, do you suppose?”
There was laughter. The guilty boy went from pink to crimson. He said nothing and was close to tears. Kolya kept him like that for a minute.

“Before you talk about a historical event like the founding of a nation, you must first understand what you mean by it,” he lectured him, in stern, cutting tones. “As for me, I attach no importance to these old wives’ tales, and I don’t think much of universal history in general,” he added carelessly, to the company at large.
“Universal history?” the captain asked, looking almost frightened.

“Yes, universal history! It’s a study of one folly of mankind after another, and nothing more. The only subjects I respect are mathematics and natural science,” said Kolya. He was showing off, and he stole a glance at Alyosha; his was the one opinion he feared there. But Alyosha was still silent and still serious. One word from Alyosha would have stopped him, but Alyosha said nothing, and “it might be the silence of contempt,” and that finally made Kolya angry.
“The classical languages too ... they’re plain madness, nothing else. You seem to disagree with me again, Karamazov?”
“I don’t agree,” said Alyosha, with a faint smile.

“The study of the classics, if you want my opinion, is just a police measure. That’s the only reason it was brought into our schools.” Gradually Kolya was growing breathless again. “They brought in Latin and Greek because they’re a bore and they numb the mind. School was dull already, so what could they do to make it duller? It was senseless enough already, so what could they do to make it more senseless? So they hit on Greek and Latin. That’s my opinion, and I hope I never change it,” Kolya finished abruptly. His cheeks were flushed.
“That’s true,” Smurov agreed suddenly, in a ringing voice of conviction. He had been listening closely.
“And yet he’s first in Latin himself,” one of the boys in the group called out suddenly.
“Yes, father, he says that, and still he’s first in Latin,” Ilusha echoed.

“What of it?” Kolya felt he had to defend himself, though the praise was very sweet to him. “I’m slogging away at Latin because I have to, because I promised my mother I’d pass my examination, and I think that whatever you do, it’s worth doing well. But deep down I have a profound contempt for the classics and all that fraud.... You don’t agree, Karamazov?”
“Why ‘fraud’?” Alyosha smiled again.

“Well, all the classical authors have been translated into every language, so it wasn’t to study the classics that they brought in Latin, but only as a police measure, to numb the intelligence. So what can you call it but a fraud?”
“Why, who taught you all this?” cried Alyosha, surprised at last.
“For one thing, I can think for myself without being taught. And besides, what I just said about the classics being translated, our teacher Kolbasnikov has said to the whole third class.”
“The doctor’s here!” cried Nina, who had said nothing until then.

A carriage belonging to Madame Hohlakov drove up to the gate. The captain, who had been waiting for the doctor all morning, rushed headlong out to meet him. “Mamma” pulled herself together and put on a dignified look. Alyosha went over to Ilusha and began straightening his pillows. From her invalid chair, Nina watched anxiously while he set the bed in order. The boys hurriedly said their goodbyes. Some promised to come back in the evening. Kolya called Perezvon, and the dog jumped down off the bed.
“I’m not going away, I’m not going away,” Kolya said hastily to Ilusha. “I’ll wait in the passage and come back when the doctor’s gone. I’ll come back with Perezvon.”

But by now the doctor had come in, an important-looking man with long dark whiskers and a shiny, clean-shaven chin, wearing a bearskin coat. On the threshold he stopped, taken aback; he probably thought he had come to the wrong place. “What is this? Where am I?” he muttered, taking off neither his coat nor his peaked sealskin cap. The crowd, the poverty of the room, the washing hung on a line in the corner, all puzzled him. The captain, bent double, was bowing low before him.
“It’s here, sir, here, sir,” he muttered, cringing. “It’s here, you’ve come to the right place, you were coming to us...”
“Sne-gi-ryov?” the doctor said loudly and pompously. “Mr. Snegiryov—is that you?”
“That’s me, sir!”
“Ah!”

Once more the doctor gave the room a squeamish look, and threw off his coat, displaying the grand decoration at his neck for all to see. The captain caught the fur coat in mid-air, and the doctor took off his cap.
“Where is the patient?” he asked emphatically.
